blocks.text: Check a lazily created shared object without locking, and lock only to create it.

Test the field without a lock; if it is `null`, enter a `synchronized` block, test **again**, and only then construct. After creation every caller takes the unsynchronized fast path. It is correct in Java only if the field is **volatile** (or the object is built from final fields only).

items: **Goal:** avoid paying for a lock on every access.
**First check:** cheap and racy by design.
**Second check:** under the lock, to stop duplicate construction.

blocks.text: Without `volatile` it is broken: another thread can see the reference before the object's fields are visible.

walkthrough.note: `instance` is `volatile`. The write that publishes it happens-before any later read that sees it, so all constructor writes are visible.
The holder idiom gets lazy, thread-safe initialization from class loading. The JVM runs `Holder`'s initializer once, on first use, with no locks in your code.
Eight threads race to call `get`. `join` makes their writes to the array visible to the main thread.
Exactly one construction happened and every thread got the same instance. The holder gives the same guarantee with less code.

blocks.text: A reporting service builds an expensive template engine.

Compiling thousands of report templates takes seconds, and most requests never need the engine. A `TemplateEngineHolder` creates it on first use. Request threads read the cached engine on every call, so a lock per read would be a visible hotspot. DCL with a volatile field keeps reads lock-free after startup.
Payoff: the lock is taken at most a few times, then every read is a single volatile load.

lists.title: Use when
items: A rarely created object is read very often by many threads.
Initialization is costly and you cannot use a holder class.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Creation is cheap: initialize eagerly in a `static final` field.
A holder class or enum works; they are simpler and provably correct.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Forgetting `volatile` compiles, usually works, and fails rarely on weak memory models.
Before Java 5, `volatile` was too weak to fix it, so old advice is wrong.
Reading the field twice on the fast path costs an extra volatile read.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: The initialization-on-demand holder idiom is lazy, thread-safe and lock-free in your code.
An `enum` singleton or a `static final` field covers most needs; reach for DCL last.

rows.difference: Singleton says there is one instance. DCL is just one way to create it lazily; a holder class or enum usually does the same job better.
If the object has only `final` fields, the JMM publishes them safely even through a racy read. Mutable state is what makes `volatile` necessary.
A read lock still costs a memory write per read. DCL's fast path is a plain volatile read, but it only covers one-time initialization.
Guarded suspension makes threads wait until a condition holds. DCL threads never wait for a condition; they only contend once, to create the object.

entries.name: Holder idiom in the JDK
entries.detail: Several JDK classes use a private nested holder class, such as lazily initialized caches built on class initialization.

entries.name: java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference
entries.detail: `updateAndGet` or `compareAndSet` achieve lock-free lazy publication when duplicate construction is tolerable.

entries.name: Suppliers.memoize
entries.detail: Wraps a `Supplier` and computes its value once, using double-checked locking with a volatile field.

entries.name: JSR-133 (Java 5)
entries.detail: The revised memory model gave `volatile` acquire/release semantics, which made volatile-based DCL correct.

options.why: An unlocked check, then a lock and a second check before creating, so later calls skip the lock.
Singleton states the goal of one instance. This is the specific locking protocol used to create it lazily.
There is no reader/writer lock; one plain monitor is used, and only for creation.
No thread waits for a condition to become true; each simply creates or reads the value.

exercises.scenario: A shared client is built on first use from a path known only at runtime, so a static holder class cannot construct it. Thousands of threads read it on a hot path, and it must be created exactly once.

options.why: Lock-free reads after creation with a volatile field; the lock is taken only while the first caller builds it.
It names the goal of one instance but gives no safe, cheap way to create it lazily.
Even a read lock adds a memory write and contention on every hot-path read, for a value created once.
Nobody needs to wait for a condition; callers simply create or read the value.

exercises.prompt: Explain why double-checked locking needs volatile, and what usually replaces it today.

modelAnswer.text: The first check reads the field without a lock, so it races with the creating thread. Without volatile there is no happens-before edge between the publishing write and that read, so a thread can see the reference but stale fields. Volatile adds the edge (correct since Java 5). A holder class or enum is simpler.

keyPoints: Unlocked first check, locked second check, create once
The unlocked read is a data race without volatile
Volatile gives a happens-before edge from publish to read (JMM, Java 5)
Partially visible objects are the failure, not double creation
Holder class or enum is the usual modern replacement
